locations.name: Empire State Building
locations.factShort: It went up in 410 days during the depths of the Depression, a pace helped along by the fact that most of its floors were identical. It then sat mostly empty for years, earning the nickname the Empty State Building.
locations.factLong: Completed in 1931 on the site of the original Waldorf-Astoria, the Empire State Building was raised in 410 days by crews working at a rate of roughly four and a half floors a week. The speed came from radical standardization: most floors were structurally identical, so steel arrived pre-cut and was riveted into place almost as fast as it could be hoisted. The Depression then kept it half-vacant for most of the 1930s, and it survived on observation-deck admissions rather than rent. It held the title of world's tallest building for 40 years, longer than any structure since.

locations.name: Yankee Stadium
locations.factShort: The current stadium opened in 2009 across the street from the 1923 original, which was demolished and turned into a public park. The old field's home plate is marked in the grass where it stood.
locations.factLong: The Yankees played in the original Yankee Stadium from 1923 until 2008, in a building so associated with Babe Ruth that it was nicknamed The House That Ruth Built. Its replacement opened in 2009 one block north, echoing the 1923 frieze that had been stripped out in a 1970s renovation. The original site became Heritage Field, a public park with three ball diamonds, where markers in the grass record where home plate and the bases once sat. From the air the two footprints are still legible side by side.

locations.name: The Wonder Wheel
locations.factShort: Built in 1920 and never once shut down for mechanical failure, the Wonder Wheel carries 24 cars, 16 of which slide along curved tracks as the wheel turns. It kept running through the decades when the rest of Coney Island was falling apart.
locations.factLong: The Wonder Wheel opened in 1920, built on site from Bethlehem Steel forged in place, and has run every season since apart from wartime and the 2020 closure. Sixteen of its 24 cars are not fixed to the rim: they roll along serpentine tracks between the hub and the outer edge, which is why riders describe the sensation as falling. It was designated a New York City landmark in 1989, near the low point of Coney Island's decline, and it outlasted almost every attraction around it. During the 1977 blackout its operator evacuated all 24 cars by hand.

locations.name: Katz's Delicatessen
locations.factShort: Open on Houston Street since 1888, Katz's still hands you a paper ticket at the door that you surrender on the way out. During the Second World War it mailed salami to soldiers overseas under the slogan it still hangs on the wall.
locations.factLong: Katz's has operated on the Lower East Side since 1888 and at its current Houston Street corner since 1917, when the Second Avenue subway construction of its day forced a move across the street. The ticket system survives from an era before cash registers were trusted: you take a ticket at the door, the counterman marks it, and losing it is famously expensive. During the Second World War the owners' sons were serving abroad, and the family began shipping salami to them, producing the slogan Send A Salami To Your Boy In The Army, which still hangs over the tables. The 1989 deli scene in When Harry Met Sally was filmed at a table the restaurant now marks with a sign.

locations.name: The Louis Armstrong House
locations.prompt: The house where Louis Armstrong lived for 28 years
locations.factShort: Armstrong could have lived anywhere and chose a modest brick house in Corona, Queens, staying from 1943 until his death in 1971. His wife Lucille bought it while he was on tour; he saw it for the first time by taxi at night.
locations.factLong: Lucille Armstrong bought the house at 34-56 107th Street in Corona in 1943 while her husband was touring, and Louis, arriving by cab in the dark, reportedly sat outside for a while before believing it was his. He lived there for the remaining 28 years of his life, declining to move to grander addresses his income could easily have covered, and became a fixture in the neighborhood who played for children on the stoop. The interiors, including Lucille's silver-and-blue kitchen, survive largely untouched. It is a National Historic Landmark and opened as a museum in 2003, with Armstrong's own reel-to-reel tape archive, hundreds of hours he recorded himself at home, held across the street.
